mcqs.q: Pemphigus is an autoimmune disease characterised by:
mcqs.explain: Pemphigus (pemphix = blister) shows intra-epithelial (suprabasilar) blistering from acantholysis.

mcqs.q: The target antigen in pemphigus vulgaris is:
mcqs.explain: Anti-desmoglein-3 IgG disrupts desmosomes between keratinocytes.

mcqs.q: The loss of cohesion between epithelial cells in pemphigus is called:
mcqs.explain: Acantholysis = breakdown of intercellular (desmosomal) adhesion.

mcqs.q: In pemphigus, the oral cavity is often described as:
opts: First to show and last to go
mcqs.explain: Oral lesions usually appear first and persist longest — 'first to show, last to go'.

mcqs.q: The histological level of the split in pemphigus vulgaris is:
mcqs.explain: Pemphigus produces a suprabasilar, intra-epithelial split with tombstone basal cells.

mcqs.q: Direct immunofluorescence of pemphigus shows a:
mcqs.explain: Intercellular 'fish-net/chicken-wire' IgG deposition is characteristic of pemphigus.

mcqs.q: The acantholytic cells seen in a pemphigus smear are called:
mcqs.explain: Rounded, free acantholytic keratinocytes are Tzanck cells.

mcqs.q: First-line treatment of pemphigus vulgaris is:
mcqs.explain: Corticosteroids are the mainstay, with immunosuppressives, plasmapheresis or rituximab as needed.

mcqs.q: Which monoclonal antibody (anti-CD20) is used in resistant pemphigus?
mcqs.explain: Rituximab (anti-CD20) depletes B cells and is effective in resistant pemphigus/pemphigoid.

mcqs.q: Mucous membrane pemphigoid is also known as:
mcqs.explain: MMP = cicatricial (benign mucous membrane) pemphigoid; it heals with scarring.

mcqs.q: The level of the split in mucous membrane pemphigoid is:
mcqs.explain: Pemphigoid splits below the epithelium at the basement membrane (lamina lucida).

mcqs.q: The antigens targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid include:
mcqs.explain: Autoantibodies target basement-membrane antigens laminin-332 and BP180.

mcqs.q: Direct immunofluorescence in mucous membrane pemphigoid shows:
opts: A linear band of IgG/C3 at the basement membrane
mcqs.explain: A linear (homogeneous) band of IgG/C3 along the basement membrane is typical of pemphigoid.

mcqs.q: Mucous membrane pemphigoid commonly presents on the gingiva as:
mcqs.explain: Painful red eroded attached gingiva = desquamative gingivitis, a common MMP presentation.

mcqs.q: Unlike pemphigus, mucous membrane pemphigoid characteristically:
mcqs.explain: Cicatricial pemphigoid heals with scarring (e.g. ocular symblepharon); pemphigus does not scar.

mcqs.q: A positive Nikolsky sign means that:
opts: Lateral pressure dislodges epithelium to form a new erosion
mcqs.explain: Nikolsky sign: shearing pressure on normal-looking skin/mucosa induces a new erosion.

mcqs.q: Epidermolysis bullosa is fundamentally a:
mcqs.explain: EB is a rare inherited disease; patients are called 'butterfly children'.

mcqs.q: The defect in epidermolysis bullosa involves:
mcqs.explain: Genetic defects of basal-cell hemidesmosomes/anchoring fibrils cause fragility and blistering.

mcqs.q: A characteristic trigger of blisters in epidermolysis bullosa is:
mcqs.explain: Even mild trauma at stress-bearing areas causes bullae; management is largely supportive (avoid trauma).

mcqs.q: The commonest ulceration of the mouth is:
mcqs.explain: Aphthous ulcers (canker sores) affect 20–60% of people — the commonest oral ulceration.

mcqs.q: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis is MORE common in:
mcqs.explain: RAS is more frequent in non-smokers and higher socioeconomic groups; HLA-B51 is associated.

mcqs.q: Minor aphthous ulcers are typically:
opts: < 0.5 cm, oval, 1–5 in number, on non-keratinised mucosa
mcqs.explain: Minor aphthae: <0.5 cm, oval, 1–5 lesions, favouring non-keratinised mucosa; heal without scarring.

mcqs.q: Which aphthous variant presents as up to 100 pinhead-sized ulcers?
mcqs.explain: Herpetiform aphthae are pinhead-sized and very numerous (1–100).

mcqs.q: Major aphthous ulcers differ from minor ones by being:
opts: Larger (>0.5 cm), crateriform and may scar
mcqs.explain: Major aphthae are >0.5 cm, ragged/crateriform, fewer but deeper, and may heal with scarring.

mcqs.q: Behçet's syndrome classically combines recurrent oral ulcers with:
mcqs.explain: Behçet's = recurrent oral + genital ulcers with ocular (and skin) involvement.

mcqs.q: Erythema multiforme is recognised clinically by its:
mcqs.explain: EM is a self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction with target (iris) skin lesions.

mcqs.q: The MINOR form of erythema multiforme is most often triggered by:
mcqs.explain: EM minor is frequently HSV-triggered; the major form/SJS is usually drug-induced or idiopathic.

mcqs.q: The severe form of erythema multiforme is also called:
mcqs.explain: EM major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome is usually caused by drugs and is more severe.

mcqs.q: A supportive home measure recommended for aphthous ulcers is:
opts: Sodium-bicarbonate mouth rinse and avoiding spicy food
mcqs.explain: Bicarbonate rinses, gentle hygiene and avoiding spicy/acidic foods help; topical steroids/analgesics for symptoms.

mcqs.q: Identify the oral lesion shown (ragged, painful mucosal erosions in an autoimmune blistering disease).
mcqs.explain: Widespread ragged painful oral erosions with suprabasilar acantholysis = pemphigus vulgaris.

mcqs.q: This direct-immunofluorescence pattern (intercellular fish-net) indicates:
mcqs.explain: An intercellular 'fish-net' IgG pattern on DIF is diagnostic of pemphigus.

mcqs.q: Identify the gingival presentation shown (red, eroded attached gingiva).
mcqs.explain: Red, eroded attached gingiva = desquamative gingivitis, common in mucous membrane pemphigoid (and lichen planus).

mcqs.q: These target/bull's-eye skin lesions indicate:
mcqs.explain: Concentric target (iris) lesions are characteristic of erythema multiforme.

saqs.q: Outline the pathogenesis and DIF finding of pemphigus vulgaris.
saqs.a: Anti-desmoglein-3 IgG → acantholysis → suprabasilar intra-epithelial split. DIF: intercellular fish-net IgG.

saqs.q: Compare pemphigus and mucous membrane pemphigoid by split level and DIF pattern.
What is a positive Nikolsky sign?
saqs.a: Lateral/shearing pressure on normal-looking mucosa or skin dislodges the epithelium to create a new erosion/blister.

saqs.q: Classify aphthous ulcers by size and number.
A patient has target skin lesions and oral erosions after a cold sore. Diagnosis and likely trigger?
Name the genetic blistering disease called 'butterfly children' and its basic defect.
saqs.a: Epidermolysis bullosa — a defect of basal-cell hemidesmosomes/anchoring fibrils causing blisters with mild trauma.
